text.p: Amgen Inc Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Gordon Binder said he is comfortable with estimates the biotech company will earn between $2.80 and $2.85 in fiscal 1997.
He said total company results will reflect a 15 percent growth rate in the sales of its Epogen drug, which boosts red blood cell counts in kidney dialysis patients.
Although a recent change in Medicare reimbursement regulations hurt Epogen sales growth during the second quarter, Binder said he sees a "very small impact" for the year as a whole.
Earlier Tuesday, Amgen reported that sales of its white blood cell boosting agent, Neupogen, rose seven percent in the second quarter, while Epogen sales rose 12 percent.

"I think the first phase (of the response to new Medicare regulations) in which dialysis centers withheld Epogen from patients is mostly behind us now," Binder said. "In the future, a small percentage of patients will get lower doses."

But he added: "Epogen was launched in 1989 and its sales growth is expected to slow each year with or without the change in reimbursement policies." Amgen did not forecast future sales of Neupogen, whose market is also maturing.
But Binder said he was unconcerned by recent studies published in the New England Journal of Medicine that questioned the therapeutic benefits of Neupogen.

"We haven't been able to see any market impact whatsoever, nor do we expect any," Binder said, noting that study looked at Neupogen being used in ways that were neither approved by the Food and Drug Administration, nor recommended by Amgen.

As markets mature for Epogen and Neupogen, the only two drugs Amgen has on the market, it is seeking to sustain growth by obtaining new indications. These include additional cancer indications for Neupogen and pediatric approval for Epogen.

But he conceded that new indications will not necessarily have a strong impact on sales since many patients, such as children with kidney failure, are already getting the drugs through off-label uses.

As for new drugs in the development pipeline, Binder said he expects the FDA probably will not act before next year on its applications for Infergen for hepatitis and a new blood cell boosting agent, Stemgen.
He said Amgen has not yet decided whether the leptin drug it has in development for obesity would best be targeted at a niche market, or to overweight people in general.
Initial trial data on the drug released last month raised concerns that it did not seem to produce sufficient weight loss to justify daily injections.

Binder said Amgen's current research on leptin is focusing on developing a next-generation form of the drug that will enable patients to receive larger amounts of it in a single injection, possibly increasing the amount of weight they could lose.
